stops.name: Strasbourg, citizen and master surgeon
stops.campa: At Strasbourg on the Rhine he buys the citizenship and enrolls in the guild of the surgeons, meaning at last to strike root and heal in one place. His cures make his name run ahead of him along the river; men come to the strange doctor who uses no bleeding and no purge but new medicines drawn by fire from the metals: his mercury, his antimony, his tinctures. He is on the threshold of the one triumph of his life. Word reaches him from Basel: the great printer Frobenius, friend of Erasmus, lies with a poisoned leg the doctors would cut off, and sends for Hohenheim.

stops.name: Basel, the saving of Froben's leg
stops.campa: The surgeons of Basel would take the leg; Theophrastus saves it. He cures Johannes Frobenius where all others have failed, and in the same house he meets and treats Erasmus of Rotterdam himself, the prince of scholars, who writes to him in wonder and thanks. On the strength of the miracle the city makes him town physician and, with it, professor at the university: the height of his fortune, a wandering bastard set in a chair of medicine. Erasmus tells him he has called Frobenius back from the shades; and for one bright season it seems the Monarch of Physicians has come into his kingdom.
stops.quote: I cannot offer thee a reward equal to thy art and knowledge; this surely I offer thee — a grateful soul. Thou hast recalled from the shades Frobenius, who is my other half.
stops.quote_source: Erasmus of Rotterdam, letter to Paracelsus at Basel, 1527

stops.name: Basel, the manifesto and the German lectures
stops.campa: He nails up a placard inviting all to his lectures and declaring war on the whole faculty: he will teach not from Galen and Avicenna but from the book of nature, and in German, the tongue of the people, so that barbers and bathkeepers and any man who would learn may come. The learned doctors are outraged that a mountebank should lecture in the vulgar tongue and open the mysteries to the mob. But the students crowd to him, and he tells them that the down on his neck knows more of physic than all the ancients, and that only he who practices an art can know it.
stops.quote: It is not titles, nor eloquence, nor the knowledge of languages, nor the reading of many books that makes a physician, but the knowledge of things and their secret virtues.
stops.quote_source: Paracelsus, opening lecture at Basel, 1527 (as reported in the tradition)

stops.name: Basel, the burning of Avicenna on Saint John's Day
stops.campa: On the eve of Saint John, when the students light the midsummer bonfire in the square, Theophrastus strides to the flames and casts into them the Canon of Avicenna, that thousand-year pillar of the schools, and with it the works of Galen: a thousand years of authority burning to ash before the crowd. Let the old books burn, he cries; reading never made a physician, and the greatest of the ancients is not worth the least of true experience. It is the boldest deed of his life and the ruin of it: the faculty will never forgive the man who burned their gods on the fire of the feast.
stops.quote: Reading never yet made a physician. Medicine is an art, and requires practice; and all that is in these books is not worth the hairs of my beard, nor of the down upon my neck.
stops.quote_source: Paracelsus at the Basel bonfire, 24 June 1527 (biographical tradition)

stops.name: Basel, the Lichtenfels suit and the flight by night
stops.campa: The fall comes swiftly. He cures the canon Cornelius von Lichtenfels of a mortal sickness for a promised hundred gulden; healed, the canon offers him six, and the court of Basel upholds the rich man against the doctor. Theophrastus answers the magistrates with such fury against their justice that they move to arrest him. In the dead of a February night he goes over the wall and out of the city, leaving his chair, his books, his instruments: a hunted man again, with only his sword and its secret pommel. The one settled year of his life is over; from here to the grave he will not stop walking.

stops.name: Colmar, the fugitive physician in Alsace
stops.campa: He comes down into Alsace and shelters a while at Colmar, taking up the cures again among strangers, guest of the physician Lorenz Fries. His fame as a healer follows him even in flight, and the sick seek out the wild doctor who works wonders with mineral medicines; but the doctors and the magistrates close against him as they did at Basel, and he cannot stay. From Colmar to Esslingen he drifts, poor, quarrelsome, and driven, writing now in his exile the books he cannot get printed, pouring into paper the whole new medicine the schools have shut their doors upon.

stops.name: Nuremberg, the guaiac war and the pen-name Paracelsus
stops.campa: At Nuremberg he throws himself against the great fraud of the age: the cure of the French disease by guaiac wood, which the Fuggers import at vast profit and the doctors prescribe though it heals no one. He writes that the poor pox-ridden are being killed for money, and prescribes his own mercury against it. The Fugger-fearing faculty has his books forbidden; the syphilis tracts are suppressed unprinted. Here, sending out an almanac of prophecy, he first signs himself Paracelsus: beyond Celsus, greater than the Roman, the name the world will keep, a wanderer's boast flung against the whole authority of the past.

stops.name: Beratzhausen, the writing of the Paragranum
stops.campa: In the little town of Beratzhausen, driven out of Nuremberg, he writes the Paragranum, the manifesto of his whole medicine: that the physician stands on four pillars: philosophy, astronomy, alchemy, and virtue, and that he who lacks any one of them is no doctor but a hangman. Here too he sets down his reading of the pox and the tartaric diseases, the stones and gravels that the body precipitates like wine throwing its lees. Unhoused and unprinted, he builds in these exile years the towering body of work that two generations after his death will overturn the medicine of Europe.
stops.quote: The four pillars on which the whole art of medicine rests are philosophy, astronomy, alchemy, and virtue; and he who would be a physician must stand upon all four.

stops.name: St Gallen, the Opus Paramirum and the dying burgomaster
stops.campa: At St Gallen he is taken in as personal physician to the ailing burgomaster Christian Studer, and in his house completes the Opus Paramirum, the great book of the three principles: that all bodies, living and dead, are compounded of Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury, and that disease is the disorder of these and healing their restoral. He dedicates a part of it to the learned Vadian, who avoids the wild doctor. Studer dies at the year's end despite his art; the town turns cold; and Theophrastus, his patron in the grave, climbs up into the mountains of Appenzell to preach and to be still.
stops.quote: Know that all the seven metals are born from a threefold matter, namely, Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt, yet in distinct and peculiar colourings.

stops.name: Appenzell, the comet and the mountain preaching
stops.campa: Among the herdsmen of the Appenzell hills he lays down the sword for the pulpit, turning lay-preacher, writing his fierce reforming theology and living close to the poor whose bodies and souls he holds to be one cure. When the great comet burns over the Alps, he reads it as a sign and writes his interpretation of it, for the heavens speak, and the wise man hears the same word in the star and in the herb. Here in the high country he is at peace as nowhere else, a physician of souls among simple folk, far from the doctors who hate him.

stops.name: Innsbruck and the Tyrol mines, barred at the gate
stops.campa: Down into the Tyrol he goes again, back to the silver and salt country of his youth, to the mines of Schwaz and Hall, gathering the last of what he needs for the book of the miners' sickness. But when he seeks to practice at Innsbruck the magistrates take one look at the ragged wandering doctor and shut the gate on him. A man in a beggar's coat cannot be the great Hohenheim. He goes on, unhoused, into the plague-country, where the fear of death opens the doors that pride keeps shut, and where his medicine will meet its hardest test among the dying.

stops.name: Sterzing, the physician in the plague
stops.campa: At Sterzing on the Brenner road the pestilence is raging when he comes, and where the guild-doctors flee, Theophrastus stays and works among the sick and dying. He writes here his tract on the plague, holding that a like cures a like: that the seed of the disease, taken in the smallest dose, arms the body against it, a doctrine two centuries before its time. He asks no fee of the poor. In the plague-towns of the Tyrol the wandering bastard is at last what he always claimed to be: not a professor but a physician, God's hand laid on the wound where the learned dare not go.
